classification.difficultyReason: Direct substitution requires signed multiplication and division, with the numerator evaluated before division and the external minus handled separately.

questions.mappingNote: Each part substitutes x=-30. Parts g and h retain the printed fraction structure; g includes the visible leading minus sign.
questions.methodNote: Examples 1 and 2 substitute negative values and evaluate using operation order. Example 2f substitutes into a fraction and divides signed integers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute a negative integer into products, differences and fractions, then evaluate in operation order.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply direct substitution while distinguishing squaring the variable from squaring the whole product, using the explicitly taught bracket and power conventions.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts require substituting x=-2. Parts e and f directly assess the distinction between -5x² and (-5x)², using the method demonstrated in Example 1.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 Example 1 substitutes a negative value into six corresponding expressions, evaluates brackets before multiplication, and distinguishes a squared pronumeral from a squared product. Page 3 continues the section's contextual substitution examples.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct negative substitution, with brackets and powers requiring the correct order of operations.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute the negative value and identify whether each power applies to the variable or an entire signed product before completing routine arithmetic.

questions.mappingNote: All nine parts evaluate expressions at a negative value. Parts e–i additionally assess powers and the placement of negative signs, so negative substitution is primary and signs of powers is secondary.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 Example 1 substitutes a negative value, evaluates brackets and powers before multiplication and addition, and distinguishes an external negative coefficient from a powered bracket. Example 2 demonstrates signed arithmetic. Page 3 continues the substitution teaching with contextual examples.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct negative substitution, including distinguishing powers of bracketed expressions from a negative coefficient outside a power.

classification.difficultyReason: Track negative signs through even and odd powers and distinguish a coefficient outside a square from a product inside a powered bracket.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts substitute z=-3; parts b, d, e and f additionally require correct treatment of powers and negative signs.
questions.methodNote: Example 1 substitutes a negative value and evaluates using the order of operations, explicitly distinguishing a negative coefficient outside a square from a parenthesised expression raised to a power. Example 2 reinforces signed multiplication.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct negative substitution, including powers and the distinction between a negative coefficient and a powered negative base.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct substitution of signed integers into sums, differences, products and quotients.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts require direct substitution of the supplied negative integers and positive integer. The offered reuse candidate has different givens and expressions, so this question is authored independently.
questions.methodNote: Example 2 substitutes signed values into sums, differences, products and quotients, then evaluates using integer sign rules. Negative substituted values are bracketed.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct substitution of signed integers into sums, differences, products and quotients.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute the given value into expressions with two powered terms, evaluate powers and products in order, and preserve the scope of leading negative signs.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts substitute the positive value w=10. Powers and negative signs are assessed within substitution, so substitute-into-expressions is primary and sign-of-powers is secondary.
questions.methodNote: Example 1 substitutes the given value and evaluates using order of operations, distinguishing a negative coefficient outside a power from a bracketed negative base. Example 2 demonstrates direct substitution into products.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct substitution, with brackets and order of operations distinguishing negative coefficients from powers.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct substitution requires tracking a negative input across separate powered terms, distinguishing an external minus from a bracketed negative and then combining results.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts require substitution of w=-2. Parts b, d, e and f also assess powers and the placement of a minus sign relative to brackets.
questions.methodNote: Example 1 substitutes a negative value and evaluates products, brackets and powers in order, distinguishing -4x² from (-4x)². Example 2 demonstrates signed arithmetic after substitution. Page 3 completes the contextual substitution examples.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct negative-number substitution, including powers and the distinction between a negative base and a negative coefficient.

classification.difficultyReason: Read horizontal then vertical positions from a labelled unit grid, assigning signs and recognising zero coordinates for points on the axes.

questions.mappingNote: Identifying seven plotted integer-coordinate points directly assesses plot-points-cartesian.
questions.methodNote: Page 5 introduces ordered horizontal and vertical coordinates, including negative coordinates. Page 6 identifies the x-coordinate first and the y-coordinate second and demonstrates plotting points on and off the axes. Page 7 continues the coordinate-plotting demonstration.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read integer coordinates from labelled points, including points on the axes.

classification.difficultyReason: Plot the supplied integer pairs using coordinate order and sign directions on a ready-labelled grid; the zero horizontal coordinate places one point on the vertical axis.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts directly assess plotting integer-coordinate points in the Cartesian plane; H additionally uses a zero horizontal coordinate.
questions.methodNote: Read the horizontal coordinate first, then the vertical coordinate. Move from the origin left or right, then up or down, and label the plotted point, following Example 5 and the coordinate explanations.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Directly plot eight integer-coordinate points, including one on the vertical axis.

classification.difficultyReason: Read the marked points from unit grids despite the surrounding picture outlines, preserving coordinate order and recognising points on axes and at the origin.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts directly assess identifying integer coordinates on Cartesian grids; plot-points-cartesian is the closest catalogue skill. None of the offered reuse candidates has the same original task or figures.
questions.methodNote: Page 5 explains horizontal then vertical coordinates using signed distances from the origin. Page 6 names the x- and y-coordinates and shows plotting, including points on axes. Page 7 supplies coordinate-reading and joined-path practice.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read integer coordinates of labelled points directly from two supplied Cartesian grids.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct figures from coordinates, classify their geometry and extract suitable bases and perpendicular heights, especially for the slanted parallelogram; also recognise perpendicular oblique lines.

questions.mappingNote: The common task is constructing figures from coordinates. Parts a, c and f additionally classify quadrilaterals and calculate areas; b and d classify triangles and calculate areas; e recognises perpendicular lines. Geometry working uses elementary base-and-height methods, with its original taught-method evidence still required.
questions.methodNote: Read the horizontal coordinate first, then the vertical coordinate; plot labelled points on equally spaced perpendicular axes and join the required straight-line intervals. The supplied teaching does not establish geometric classification, area formulas or the geometric test for perpendicular lines.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct coordinate figures, recognise their geometric properties and use perpendicular heights to calculate areas.

classification.difficultyReason: Infer reflection from the partially supplied second petal, extend the symmetry to two further petals, and translate those constructions back into ordered coordinate lists.

questions.mappingNote: The task directly assesses plotting and joining ordered coordinates, extended to constructing congruent petals using symmetry. The answer graph corroborates the intended symmetric construction, but original teaching evidence for that extension remains missing.
questions.methodNote: Pages 5–6 teach horizontal-then-vertical coordinate plotting; Example 6 on pages 6–7 teaches joining coordinate lists in order. No explicit coordinate-reflection method is supplied.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Complete coordinate pairs and construct four congruent petals in different quadrants.

classification.difficultyReason: Uses the prescribed substitution–table–coordinates–plot sequence, preserving signs and locating half-unit outputs on the axes. These are routine linked procedures; the fractional values introduce no new strategic decision.

questions.mappingNote: Question 2a–d directly connects linear equations, tables, coordinates and graphs; linear-representations is the most advanced directly assessed catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Substitute each supplied x into the rule, retain exact halves, form ordered pairs in table-column order, then plot horizontal coordinate first and vertical coordinate second. Example 7 demonstrates the table–coordinates–plot sequence.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Connect four linear rules with tables, ordered pairs and plots involving half-integer coordinates.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct substitution of specified integer inputs into two linear rules.

questions.mappingNote: Question 3 directly assesses completing value tables; Example 7 supplies the table method and Example 1 supplies signed substitution.
questions.methodNote: Substitute each input into the rule, respecting negative signs and order of operations, and record the output in the corresponding table cell.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct substitution of specified integer inputs into two linear rules.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluates signed inputs, including subtracting inside brackets before squaring, then converts the completed tables into ordered pairs and plots. The nonlinear outcome is supplied, so no inference about curve shape or transformation is required.

questions.mappingNote: Example 7 establishes table-to-coordinate-to-plot order; Example 5 establishes point placement and Example 1 distinguishes brackets and powers. Question 4 extends that same procedure to nonlinear rules.
questions.methodNote: Substitute into the rule to complete the table, list each (x,y) pair, then plot horizontal followed by vertical displacement. Evaluate parentheses before squaring.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate squared expressions, form ordered pairs and construct plots that are not straight lines.

classification.difficultyReason: Infer linear rules from tables, including negative multipliers and constant terms, and express each rule in words and algebra.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts directly assess finding a rule relating the two rows of a table, followed by verbal and algebraic expression of that rule.
questions.methodNote: Example 8 describes multiplying the input and adding a constant, then expresses this in algebra. Example 10 demonstrates a negative multiplier. Infer the operation from corresponding table entries and check the resulting rule.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Infer linear rules from tables, including negative multipliers and constant terms, and express each rule in words and algebra.

classification.difficultyReason: Extend the two-chair increase, plot table values and express the relationship as c=2t+2, accounting for the two end chairs. The supplied values and staged prompts make these routine linked procedures.

questions.mappingNote: Question 3 follows Example 9's sequence directly, using tables and chairs in place of tiles.
questions.methodNote: Example 8 expresses table rules as multiplication followed by addition. Example 9 counts a growing pattern, completes its table, identifies the constant increase, plots separate ordered pairs and states a multiply-and-add rule.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Connect a growing table-and-chair pattern with a value table, plotted points and an algebraic rule.

classification.difficultyReason: Beyond extending and graphing the decreasing counts, determine when the shrinking foot stops projecting beyond the two-can-wide upright. This requires connecting the spatial change to a stopping condition that the total-can rule alone does not supply.

questions.mappingNote: This question directly connects a can pattern, values, coordinates and a rule; linear-representations is the closest assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 9 counts successive shapes, extends a table using a constant change, plots the ordered pairs as discrete points and describes a multiply-and-add rule. Example 8 connects a table with an algebraic rule; Example 10 supports plotting coordinates and recognising a negative relationship. Page 3 supplies subtraction and contextual interpretation evidence.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Connect a decreasing spatial pattern with a table, plotted coordinates and an equation, then interpret when the shape ceases to be an L.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate monthly spending into d=1000-20m, use it for a later balance and reverse the relationship to find when the funds run out. The table scaffolds the routine subtraction model.

questions.mappingNote: Sarah's balance decreases by 20 each month from 1000; extend the table, state the rule and apply it.
questions.methodNote: Example 4 models money remaining by subtracting repeated withdrawals; Example 8 finds a rule from corresponding table values.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Model a monthly decrease, evaluate the rule and determine how long the funds last.

classification.difficultyReason: Read the five-hours-per-week rate directly from the supplied table, express h=5w and apply multiplication or inverse division. The table removes the need to derive the weekly rate from the journey times.

questions.mappingNote: The given table establishes 5 hours per week. Continue that pattern, write h=5w and apply the rule.
questions.methodNote: Example 8 identifies a multiplicative relationship between paired table values; Example 9 extends a constant-step table and writes its rule.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise a constant weekly increase, write a rule and use multiplication and division.

classification.difficultyReason: Read plotted coordinates and distinguish the listed rules using the value at x=0 and the change in y per unit x. Separating the three decreasing rules requires checking both features, with the candidate list providing scaffolding.

questions.mappingNote: Question 8 reverses this representation process: read supplied plotted coordinates, identify the output at x = 0 and the change per unit input, then select the corresponding listed rule.
questions.methodNote: Examples 8–10 connect tables, plotted coordinates and rules by describing how the output changes with the input; Example 10 explicitly includes negative values and y = -2x.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Match six plotted linear relationships to equations, distinguishing their rates of change and values at x = 0.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct substitution of supplied integers into sums, differences, products and a quotient.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct substitution of supplied integers into sums, differences, products and a quotient.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the taught horizontal-then-vertical plotting procedure on a supplied labelled grid, using signs for direction and zero coordinates for points on axes.

classification.difficultyReason: Form expressions for repeated withdrawals and evaluate a balance that can become negative.

classification.difficultyReason: Express a repeated temperature decrease algebraically, substitute fractional values and determine the time needed to reach a specified temperature.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify multiplication and addition or subtraction rules from tables, including negative multipliers.

questions.methodNote: Pages 5–6 establish horizontal coordinate first and vertical coordinate second. Pages 9–10 demonstrate converting table columns into ordered pairs and plotting separate points. Pages 12–13 demonstrate describing a table relationship and expressing it algebraically.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Connect a fixed-total sharing situation with a completed table, eleven coordinates, a graph and an algebraic rule.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Connect a fixed-total sharing context with a table, ordered pairs, a discrete plot and an algebraic rule.

classification.difficultyReason: Infer missing square vertices, including both orientations and a square with an oblique given side.

classification.difficultyReason: Infer the missing rectangle width from its area and give both possible coordinate configurations.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Infer the missing rectangle width from its area and give both possible coordinate configurations.

classification.difficultyReason: Enumerate whole-stack combinations preserving 30 pieces of fruit, recognise that one mango stack replaces two pineapple stacks, and translate the table into coordinates, a plot and y=6-2x. Supplied endpoints support the enumeration.

questions.methodNote: Read ordered pairs horizontally then vertically; convert table rows into coordinates and plot them. Find a rule by describing the operation connecting the quantities, as in Examples 8 and 9.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Connect whole stacks of two fruits with a fixed total through a table, coordinates, a plot and a rule.

classification.difficultyReason: Restrict the given equation to nonnegative whole-person counts, identify feasible adult values giving integer child counts, and plot the pairs. Then select pairs matching each group total; the earlier enumeration scaffolds this interpretation.

questions.mappingNote: The ticket context assesses a real-life linear relationship through integer coordinates, plotting and interpretation. Pages 2, 5–6 and 9–10 supply substitution, coordinate and table-to-plot methods; page 12 provides further rule context.
questions.methodNote: Substitute numerical values into a rule, list the resulting coordinate pairs and plot horizontal then vertical coordinates. Select the required combinations from the feasible pairs using their totals; no simultaneous-equation method is introduced.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find all feasible integer pairs for a ticket-cost relationship, plot them and select pairs satisfying a total-person constraint.

classification.difficultyReason: Read side length a from the square's vertex coordinates, formulate s=a², evaluate the supplied values and plot the resulting pairs using suitable scales. Non-collinearity is stated, so no independent explanation of the curved relationship is required.

questions.mappingNote: Plotting fractional coordinate pairs is the most advanced directly assessed catalogue skill. The square-area rule and its evaluation are prerequisites within parts a–b.
questions.methodNote: Substitute values into an expression, retain exact fractions, form coordinate pairs from the two table rows, and plot horizontal coordinate first and vertical coordinate second. Pages 5–6 establish coordinate order; pages 9–10 connect tables and plots. Original square-area prerequisite teaching is absent.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Connect a square's algebraic area rule with fractional side lengths, a value table and a plot.
